issues.legal_issue: A vendor’s admission of the sale agreement and substantial payment of its consideration can establish the basis for specific performance without further proof of those admitted matters.
material_facts: The vendor admitted executing the sale agreement and receiving a substantial part of the sale consideration.
The trial court granted specific performance, and the Supreme Court held that no further evidence or proof of the admitted execution and receipt was required.
issues.conclusion: The trial court was right to grant specific performance on the basis of the vendor’s admissions.
issues.legal_principle: In a suit for specific performance, where the vendor specifically admits execution of the agreement and receipt of substantial advance consideration, the purchaser need not further prove those admitted matters. The Court relied on the trial court’s findings and did not cite an earlier case for this proposition.

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The buyer brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.vendor_admitted_contract_execution: The vendor admitted executing the agreement to sell.
predicates.vendor_admitted_substantial_payment: The vendor admitted receiving a substantial part of the agreed sale consideration.

issues.definition: When a buyer seeks specific performance and the vendor admits both execution of the agreement and substantial payment, the admitted matters establish the basis for specific performance.

issues.legal_issue: A subsequent transferee need not have the later transfer formally cancelled for a court to declare it not binding in a specific-performance suit when the transfer is directly in issue and the parties have litigated it.
material_facts: The buyer challenged sale deeds executed after the agreement to sell and alleged that they were nominal and intended to defeat her rights.
The trial court framed specific issues concerning the later sale deeds, the parties led evidence on those issues, and the trial court found the deeds not binding on the vendor and the buyer.
The High Court set aside that part of the decree because the buyer had not sought a specific cancellation relief.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in holding that the trial court could not declare the later sale deeds not binding in the absence of a specific prayer for their cancellation; the trial court’s decree was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act did not prevent the declaration in these circumstances because the later deeds were directly in issue, specific issues had been framed, and evidence had been led. Under Lala Durga Prasad v. Lala Deep Chand, the proper form of decree is to direct specific performance between the vendor and buyer and require the subsequent transferee to join in the conveyance to pass title; Rathnavathi v. Kavitha Ganashamdas followed that approach.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and subsequent_transfer_challenged_in_suit and specific_issues_framed_on_transfer and parties_led_evidence_on_transfer

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The buyer brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.subsequent_transfer_challenged_in_suit: The buyer challenged a transfer made after the agreement to sell as affecting the buyer’s rights.
predicates.specific_issues_framed_on_transfer: The court framed specific issues concerning the later transfer.
predicates.parties_led_evidence_on_transfer: The parties presented evidence concerning the later transfer.

issues.definition: When a buyer seeking specific performance challenges a later transfer and the parties litigate specific issues about it with evidence, the transfer may be declared not binding without a separate cancellation prayer.

issues.legal_issue: Where later purchasers’ deeds are alleged to be nominal transfers intended to defeat an earlier agreement, the purchasers must establish payment of the consideration stated in those deeds when the surrounding circumstances support the allegation.
material_facts: The later sale deeds were executed after the agreement to sell and were alleged to have been made to defeat the buyer’s rights.
The later purchasers were related to the person who executed the deeds, and the trial court found that the stated sale consideration had not been proved.
The trial court found the later deeds to be nominal, and the Supreme Court upheld that finding.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the later deeds were nominal and not binding on the vendor and the buyer was justified because the later purchasers failed to prove payment of the stated consideration.
issues.legal_principle: On the facts, where later transfers were alleged to be nominal and intended to defeat rights under an earlier agreement, the party relying on those transfers was required to prove payment of their stated consideration. The Court relied on the trial court’s findings on the evidence; it cited no separate earlier case for this evidentiary proposition.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and later_transfer_after_contract and later_transfer_alleged_to_be_nominal and transfer_recipients_failed_to_prove_consideration

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The buyer brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.later_transfer_after_contract: The transfer was made after the agreement to sell.
predicates.later_transfer_alleged_to_be_nominal: A party alleged that the later transfer was nominal and intended to defeat rights under the earlier agreement.
predicates.transfer_recipients_failed_to_prove_cons: The persons relying on the later transfer failed to establish payment of its stated consideration.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance proceeding, a later transfer made after the contract and alleged to be nominal is treated as nominal and not binding when those relying on it fail to prove its stated consideration.

issues.legal_issue: The discretionary nature of specific performance does not justify denying relief merely because the property was later transferred where the vendor admitted the earlier agreement and the later transfers were knowingly made and found to be nominal.
material_facts: The vendor admitted the earlier agreement and receipt of substantial advance consideration.
The person who arranged the later transfers knew of the agreement and transferred the property to relatives of his own.
The trial court found the later deeds to be nominal, and the Supreme Court held that the trial court had rightly granted specific performance.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in using the discretionary character of specific performance to reverse the decree; the trial court’s decree was restored.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the discretion governing specific performance under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act and held that, on these facts, the trial court had rightly exercised it. The admitted agreement, substantial advance payment, knowledge of the agreement, and nominal nature of the later deeds did not justify denying specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and vendor_admitted_contract_execution and vendor_admitted_substantial_payment and later_transferee_knew_of_contract and later_transfer_found_nominal

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The buyer brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.vendor_admitted_contract_execution: The vendor admitted executing the agreement to sell.
predicates.vendor_admitted_substantial_payment: The vendor admitted receiving a substantial part of the agreed sale consideration.
predicates.later_transferee_knew_of_contract: The person who arranged the later transfer knew of the earlier agreement to sell.
predicates.later_transfer_found_nominal: The court found that the later transfer was nominal.

issues.definition: When a vendor admits the earlier agreement and substantial payment, and a later transfer made with knowledge of the agreement is found nominal, the discretion in a specific-performance proceeding is exercised in the buyer’s favor.
